extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP policymakers, academics and researchers interested in patent law and AI-related disclosure issues
extracted.subtask_short: patent disclosure sufficiency for AI inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment and guidance on the patent-law disclosure/enablement requirement as applied to inventions involving artificial intelligence — including AI-generated inventions, AI techniques as inventions, and inventions that require AI to work. Discusses jurisdictional standards, reproducibility and explainability concerns, and practical evidentiary issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient disclosure / enablement (general standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental patentability requirement across jurisdictions. The disclosure should enable reproduction of the invention and distinguish true inventions from speculative concepts. Failure to sufficiently disclose can make a patent unenforceable or revocable. See Article 83 EPC, Art.14(3) UK Patents Act, 35 U.S.C. §112 (Specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must set out at least one mode for carrying out the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The description should set out at least one mode for carrying out the invention claimed, using examples where appropriate and with reference to drawings, if any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples and drawings help persons skilled in the art to make or use the invention. Omitting a mode or examples may lead to insufficiency findings because the specification fails to show how to implement the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries (such as the United States), the description is required to disclose the best mode for carrying out the invention known to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §112 the inventor must set forth the best mode contemplated. This is a US-specific objective of disclosure and may influence sufficiency/enforceability analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: absence of undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy enablement, a patent specification must disclose the invention in sufficient detail to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make it without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is assessed against the knowledge of a person skilled in the art. If undue experimentation would be required to practice the invention from the disclosure, the specification may fail the enablement requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional sufficiency grounds and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Insufficient disclosure is a ground for opposition, revocation, or invalidity (e.g., Article 100(b) and Article 138(1)(b) EPC; Section 72 UK Patents Act; 35 U.S.C. §112 issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different jurisdictions articulate remedies (opposition, revocation) and statutory formulations, but all treat inability to carry out the invention as a serious defect. Practitioners should cite the relevant statutory articles when arguing insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability core criteria (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability, subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be novel, involve an inventive step (not obvious to a person skilled in the art), be industrially applicable (useful), and fall within patentable subject matter defined by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These substantive criteria are distinct from disclosure but interact with it (e.g., disclosure helps define the metes and bounds of the claimed invention and may affect obviousness analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subject matter is commonly excluded from patentability: discoveries of natural materials, scientific theories or mathematical methods, certain biological subject-matter (jurisdiction-dependent), schemes or rules (business methods, mental acts), and methods contrary to public order or health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional variations apply. Authors list TRIPS Article 27.2–3 style exceptions; practitioners must check local law for specifics on exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / non-obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, with regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art; the difference must be both inventive (creative) and a noticeable step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions frame this as an 'advance' or 'progress' over prior art and require that the advance be significant and essential to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability / utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be capable of being applied for practical purposes — products must be makeable and processes must be practicable or 'usable' in industry (broadly defined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely theoretical ideas or purely intellectual/aesthetic activities are typically not patentable; industrial applicability includes agriculture in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability of AI (transparency desideratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explainable AI produces details or reasons that make its functioning clear or easy to understand; lack of explainability (the 'black-box' problem) arises from complexity and/or high dimensionality of models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different ML techniques vary in explainability (e.g., decision trees are more transparent; deep neural networks and SVMs less so). Legal and public demands for reason-giving can be satisfied by explaining an algorithm's purpose, design, and basic functioning, although patent law itself does not require disclosure of an AI's internal decision processes beyond enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility requirement for AI-involved inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducibility requires sufficient information (e.g., code, datasets, hardware, computational power, hyper-parameter settings, provenance/lineage) so that others can recreate a machine-learning workflow and reach the same conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-learning research faces reproducibility crises; lacking details on artifacts and settings can defeat enablement. For patents, inability of others to reproduce the invention supports an insufficiency challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-created inventions: inventorship vs disclosure distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-generated inventions (inventions conceived independently by software with no human inventive contribution) raise inventorship and ownership issues but do not necessarily negate the disclosure requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes high-profile cases (e.g., DABUS) where offices rejected AI as inventor; disclosure itself is a separate issue — the patent system may still require enablement regardless of who/what conceived the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI technique as invention (AI-inventions): subject-matter eligibility concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: When the AI technique itself is the claimed invention, questions primarily arise about subject-matter eligibility (e.g., medical AI systems, algorithms), though disclosure per se may be less directly challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patenting AI techniques can face uncertainties about whether the subject matter is statutory patentable subject matter; practitioners must consider eligibility doctrines alongside disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: When working an invention requires application of AI: sufficiency pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: If practicing the claimed invention requires applying an AI technique, three problematic situations arise: (1) the AI technique is not disclosed (claims unsupported), (2) the invention is reproducible but the AI's workings are unexplainable, and (3) the AI-dependent invention cannot be reproduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situation (1) implicates enablement (claims must be supported by the description). Situation (2) may raise explainability concerns but, per the article, patent law does not require inner workings explanation beyond enablement. Situation (3) triggers insufficiency because the invention cannot be carried out by a person skilled in the art without undue experimentation or access to undisclosed artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on AI by a person skilled in the art to work the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person of ordinary skill must resort to using an AI (not disclosed in the specification) to make the invention work, this indicates the original disclosure may be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, courts/examiners will assess whether the skilled person can carry out the invention from the disclosure and their common general knowledge without needing an undisclosed AI; needing an undisclosed AI undercuts the disclosure bargain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Datasets, proprietary artifacts and trade secrecy vs disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AI inventions require additional and specific datasets or proprietary artifacts for disclosure and reproduction; owners may refuse to disclose valuable data, undermining sufficiency and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where essential datasets or training material are withheld as trade secrets, the patent may fail to enable reproduction. Balancing inventor rights and public benefit may require legal and technical solutions (e.g., deposit mechanisms, anonymization, detailed metadata).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the disclosure requirement (contract theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent disclosure aims to give the public sufficient knowledge to practice and build on the invention in return for granting a temporary monopoly — a contractual exchange between inventor and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure objectives include promoting diffusion of knowledge, aiding examiners, clarifying claim boundaries for competitors, distinguishing real inventions from speculation, and promoting technology transfer. If AI undermines this exchange, the social-contract justification of patents is threatened.
